title: Street Trees and Summer Heat: Evidence from Ashworth

headings.text: Street Trees and Summer Heat: Evidence from Ashworth

key_sentences: Neighbourhoods in Ashworth with more tree canopy were markedly cooler on hot summer afternoons.
The effect is largest in dense residential streets, which are also where canopy is scarcest.
Trees cool streets in two ways: they shade surfaces that would otherwise store heat, and they release water vapour through their leaves.
The council installed 52 shaded air-temperature sensors on lamp posts in May 2024.
The cooling associated with canopy is roughly twice as large in streets with terraced housing as in streets of detached houses.
Even so, the size of the effect is in line with studies from other temperate cities.

list_items.text: 1. Prioritise planting where canopy is lowest and heat exposure is highest:
(i) the Old Town and the terraced streets of Riverside;
(ii) routes to schools, clinics and care homes.
2. Protect existing mature trees, which provide far more shade than new planting for at least fifteen years.
3. Keep the sensor network running so that the effect of new planting can be measured directly.
[1] Ashworth City Council (2023). Urban Forest Strategy 2023–2040. Ashworth: City Council.
[2] Lindqvist, M. and Ferreira, A. (2021). Canopy cover and street-level air temperature in five northern cities. Journal of Urban Climate Studies 14(2), 88–104.
[3] Weller, T. (2025). A low-cost sensor network for urban heat. Calderbrook Working Paper 25/03.
